entry.title: Autoresearch as Optimization
entry.content:
An agent edits a program, runs an experiment, and gets a better score. It repeats the process. Early progress comes quickly; later, the edits become smaller and the score barely moves. The agent is still working. What would make the next hour useful?

This question connects several recent papers on LLMs for scientific discovery. Some redesign the search over candidate solutions. Others change what agents remember, how they divide work, or how they measure progress. I find it useful to read them together: each changes how a research system spends its next unit of effort.

The examples here involve computational discovery, where programs, models, and algorithms can be tested repeatedly. They make a broader question concrete: how can a system accumulate useful evidence without becoming trapped by the path that produced it?

Search over ideas

A comment by tsuname compares autoresearch methods with familiar optimization ideas: momentum, cross-entropy search, simulated annealing. It is a useful starting point. Once a model can propose meaningful edits, the remaining choices look like questions an optimizer must answer: where to sample, which results to retain, and when to leave a promising neighborhood.

For a fixed task, I would describe the loop with the following bookkeeping:

\[C_t=\mathcal M(H_t),\qquad x_{t+1}\sim p_\theta(\cdot\mid C_t),\qquad y_{t+1}=f(x_{t+1}).\]

$H_t$ is the research record; $\mathcal M$ chooses what enters the context $C_t$; the model proposes candidate $x$; the evaluator returns $y$. With budget $B$, the search aims for a strong best verified candidate:

\[\mathbb E\!\left[\max_{t:\,\text{cost}(1{:}t)\leq B} f(x_t)\right].\]

This view separates improving a candidate from changing how candidates are proposed. Even with frozen model weights, the system can adapt its search through parent selection, context, and experiment allocation. The equations describe that interface; they do not assume an analytic gradient through a running program.

Consider a packing solver. Changing a tie-breaking rule and replacing the entire placement strategy can both be short code edits. Their distance in lines of code says little about their distance as ideas. That makes the representation of search experience especially important.

Two earlier papers give useful ways to think about it. DeltaEvolve represents program history through semantic deltas: descriptions of what changed and whether it helped. Future proposals receive these changes as inspiration. Its momentum analogy is about carrying useful directions forward. It does not imply that natural-language edits are numerical gradients. A compact account of an improvement can be more useful than another full snapshot of the program.

Contrastive Concept-Tree Search instead organizes programs through a hierarchy of concepts. It fits distributions to concepts in high- and low-performing programs using cross-entropy updates, then uses their likelihood ratio to guide parent selection. The comparison is informative: a concept common in good programs may also be common everywhere. Contrasting good and bad outcomes helps identify which concepts distinguish them. The learned sampling statistics live in concept space; this is not an LLM weight update.

There is also a distinction between accepting a temporary regression and preserving the best result. An annealing-style search can move through weaker candidates while keeping a separate incumbent. Likewise, a research system can give an unfinished direction time to mature without replacing its best verified artifact. The optimization analogy is most useful when it exposes these choices explicitly.

What should survive?

The search record has two jobs that can conflict. It preserves discoveries, but it also conditions the next proposal. A long account of failed approaches may prevent repetition. It may also convince the agent that a broader direction has been exhausted when only one implementation failed.

This is where optimization and agent architecture meet. In the notation above, changing $\mathcal M$ changes the proposal distribution even if $\theta$ stays fixed. Memory policy affects where the search goes.

Fork-and-Flush studies runs that remain in localized regions of idea space. It periodically copies the accumulated workspace into parallel continuations with fresh chat contexts, gives each time to explore, and continues the best branch. Forking provides alternatives; flushing changes the history conditioning each alternative. Its ablations find gains from each operation and a larger gain from their combination. The paper also visualizes a polyomino trajectory that moves beyond the region occupied by local refinements.

Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting makes a stronger reset. At round boundaries, the communicating team retains the best candidate and its score, discards agent sessions and the other candidate history, and starts again. The experiments span heuristic programming, kernel optimization, and model training. The useful distinction is what crosses the boundary: the successful artifact survives, while the path used to find it is removed from the active search state.

Stateless Language Agents makes context reconstruction routine. The harness retains candidates and measured outcomes; every Advisor and Worker invocation starts fresh. The Advisor receives evidence across directions and assigns experiments. Workers receive their assignment, local candidate, and focused feedback. State persists outside the conversations. The harness also distinguishes an evaluated non-improvement from an inconclusive execution failure, so the Advisor can reason about what was actually tested.

These designs suggest a practical separation between the artifact, evidence about it, and the conversation that produced it. Each can have a different lifetime. Keeping the artifact preserves progress. Keeping testable evidence can prevent repeated mistakes. Keeping every interpretation may preserve assumptions that deserve another look.

The hard case is a failed experiment. “This idea does not work” and “this implementation never ran correctly” are different observations. If both become a negative entry in memory, future search may avoid an unexplored direction. If both disappear, the next agent may waste its budget repeating the same error. I would want a memory policy to preserve the reason a conclusion is justified, while allowing the conclusion itself to be reconsidered.

The cost of feedback

More promising candidates help only if we can evaluate enough of them. A search with an hour-long test has a very different budget from one with a one-second test. The cost of feedback determines how many sequential decisions can fit into the run.

DuoDiscover co-discovers optimization targets and cheap proxy evaluators, called yardsticks. Workers iterate against these proxies, while true evaluations confirm gains and recheck proxy fidelity. An orchestrator coordinates the workers. A yardstick must rank candidates usefully; its score need not match the true score. This saves time only when a faithful proxy exists and its construction cost is worthwhile.

This changes how I would compare research systems. Candidate count alone hides the quality and cost of feedback. Parallel workers may reduce elapsed time, while a cheaper evaluator may also permit more rounds of dependent experimentation. These are different ways of spending compute. A useful comparison needs to show what the budget buys: proposals, verified experiments, or opportunities to act on new evidence.

Learning the next experiment

The systems above expose decisions that could themselves be learned: which direction to pursue, what evidence to retrieve, and when to stop. The training target matters. An experiment that fails to improve the incumbent can still make a later breakthrough possible.

MIRA separates an outer research decision from the executor carrying it out. MIRA-AC trains a shared generative actor–critic at those decision boundaries. The critic forecasts remaining return; policy learning targets the research decision response, while execution remains fixed. Under its proxy feedback, reward is an increase in best-so-far quality, so later gains can be credited across a sequence of investigations.

A concrete example is its physics discovery task. The outer policy asks for an experiment that independently varies a particle parameter, allowing the executor to distinguish competing interaction laws. The decision is useful because it asks a discriminating question. That is a more specific learning target than simply generating another plausible modification.

IdeaScientist trains a different part of research. It separately trains gap-finding, innovation, and report-writing roles with GRPO, using reference-grounded rewards, and then combines them under a fixed orchestrator. Its main output is a research proposal. It asks how to produce better ideas before execution; MIRA-AC asks how to choose investigations as experimental evidence accumulates. Both are relevant, but proposal quality and experimental progress require different evidence.

For test-time training, I am especially interested in the gap between immediate score and future usefulness. A policy can become good at producing valid candidates and still rarely change the best result. Learning which experiments create opportunities for later progress seems closer to the behavior we want from a research agent.

Where to go next

I would judge a discovery system by what happens after its first plateau. Does it keep producing variants of the same idea? Can it tell whether a direction failed or merely lacked a working implementation? Does a restart recover exploration, or just repeat the opening moves?

A useful next experiment would begin from the same checkpoint and spend the same remaining budget under different memory policies. Compare the best verified result, but also inspect the sequence of decisions: which hypotheses changed, which experiments ruled something out, and which findings survived the reset. Code-edit size alone cannot establish that the agent explored a new idea.

There is a similar experiment to run on feedback. Keep the proposal mechanism fixed and vary how the system purchases evidence: full evaluations, cheap proxies with calibration, or targeted tests that distinguish competing explanations. The most valuable test may be the one that changes the next decision, even when its immediate score is unimpressive.

The question I want to carry forward is simple: what should a research system learn from an unsuccessful experiment, and what should it be willing to forget?
entry.summary: How search, memory, and feedback shape what language-model agents discover.

entry.title: Revisiting PPO for LLM Post-Training
entry.content:
A model can get better at producing working code while barely improving the best solution it has found. That gap is what interests me about PPO for test-time training.

In post-training, we usually want a model to perform well across many questions. In test-time discovery, we spend a budget on one problem, learn from our attempts, and keep the best result. A training method that improves the average response may still struggle to make the next discovery.

Recent work on PPO offers several ways to rethink that loop: how we sample, what the critic learns, and how much we trust an update. We have started testing these ideas by training a small model to guide a larger one through a programming search.

Revisiting PPO

PPO gives the actor and critic different jobs. The actor learns which actions to make more likely. The critic estimates the return expected from the current prompt and generated prefix, providing a baseline for the actor’s update.

Two updates, different interventions

For actor $\pi_ heta$ and critic $V_\phi$, write $\psi_ heta= abla_ heta\log\pi_ heta(a\mid s)$. Their updates expose the main components:

\[ egin{aligned} g_{\mathrm{actor}}&=\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}\!\left[m\,\hat A\,(w\psi_ heta-c(s)) ight],\[4pt] L_V&=\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}\!\left[m^V\omega_x\,\ell(V_\phi(s),Y) ight]. \end{aligned}\]

$\mathcal D$: sampled trajectories · $m,m^V$: masks and aggregation · $\hat A$: advantage · $w$: probability correction · $c$: score correction · $\omega_x,Y$: critic weight and target. This is a component map: clipping enters through effective weights/masks; KL terms are omitted.

Work Main intervention
SAO $\mathcal D$: one rollout per prompt; $\hat A$: skip-observation GAE; $w$: strict token masking; more frequent critic updates.
FlashREINFORCE $\hat A_i=R_i- ar R_{\mathrm{batch}}$; single rollouts, sequence admission, per-trajectory averaging; no $L_V$.
AC2 $\hat A_i=v_i- ar v$, $Y= ar v$; critic-ready problems use $v_i=V(s\cdot c_i)$ for unfinished chunks.
TEMPO $\hat A_t=V(y_{\mathrm{complete}})-V(s_t)$; periodically recalibrate $V$ on labeled data.
Score Centering $c(s)=\mathbb E_{a\sim\mu(\cdot\mid s)}[w\psi_ heta]$: center the weighted score under the sampler $\mu$.
Decoupled PPO Separate $ u/\mu$ for behavior correction from $\pi_ heta/ u$ for PPO clipping; $ u$ is a recent policy.
EasyPPO $\omega_x\propto1/\max(\hat\sigma_x,\varepsilon)$; $m^V$ retains truncated samples; smaller critic minibatches.

For complete terminal-return PPO with $\gamma=\lambda=1$, $\hat A_t=R-V_{\mathrm{old}}(s_t)$. Reward centering changes $\hat A$; score centering changes the gradient term $c(s)$.

These papers use the critic in different ways. A baseline reduces variance after we observe an outcome. A learned evaluator supplies feedback when a real outcome is unavailable or expensive. The second role asks much more of the model.

For our first discovery experiments, we kept the critic in the baseline role and evaluated every generated program. This lets us study what PPO learns from real execution feedback before asking the critic to replace any of it.

What makes TTT special?

One problem, many attempts

Here, sample = 1 at the task level. We adapt to one target problem, rather than training over a broad collection of unrelated questions. We can still generate many candidates and evaluate them on many cases. All those attempts serve the same search.

This also changes the input distribution. Each successful revision becomes a possible starting point for the next attempt. The model learns while the problem in front of it changes.

We keep the best of all attempts

At the end, we want the strongest verified solution found anywhere in the history. The objective is closer to:

\[\mathbb E\!\left[\max_{1\leq k\leq N} S(c_k) ight],\]

where later candidates can depend on earlier results. Repeatedly producing a good existing solution helps average reward but adds little to that maximum. We need enough reliability to keep the search moving, alongside a willingness to try changes that might fail.

Discovery needs depth

An experiment often reveals what to try next. Generating a large batch before receiving feedback delays that process: every candidate in the batch starts from the same available history.

With a fixed candidate budget, larger batches leave fewer rounds to learn from the results. Smaller batches give later attempts more opportunities to build on earlier discoveries.

Parallel exploration still matters, and smaller batches can make updates noisier. The question is how much breadth we can afford before sacrificing useful feedback depth. We have yet to test that tradeoff with a matched-budget batch-size study.

PPO for discovery

We used Reef to search for C++ solutions to FrontierCS Polyomino packing. A Qwen3-8B editor proposed natural-language guidance; a frozen GPT-OSS-120B executor turned it into code. Training changed the editor, while the executor stayed fixed.

Each round selected eight parent programs from the search history and sampled 16 guidance responses per parent: 128 candidates per round. The editor could generate up to 10,240 tokens, including thinking. We evaluated programs on 70 cases and returned scores and error feedback to the search history.

We compared PPO with Guidance-TTT, our group-based discovery recipe. PPO used a learned critic, five critic-only warmup rounds, and an exponential transform of the program score as reward. Guidance-TTT used adaptive-entropic, leave-one-out advantages to emphasize stronger candidates within each group. Both started from the same editor model and seed program.

The first 30 rounds give each method 3,840 candidate attempts:

Method Best score by round 30 Mean score, rounds 16–30 Valid programs, rounds 16–30
Guidance-TTT 80.45 68.23 93.4%
PPO 78.48 74.28 96.6%

Means include failed candidates. These are initial results from one run per configuration, using the same cases throughout search. PPO trained full parameters while Guidance-TTT used LoRA; their learning rates and regularization also differed. The comparison therefore describes the two systems, without isolating the effect of the critic.

What we achieved

PPO produced working programs consistently and maintained higher average quality in the later half of the shared 30-round window. Most attempts reached evaluation successfully, even though the model we trained only wrote guidance for another model.

That is a useful property for discovery. Broken implementations consume budget and interrupt the chain of experiments. An editor that can propose executable changes gives us a stronger base to build on.

The best-score curve tells a different story. Guidance-TTT reached 80.45, while PPO reached 78.48. Reliable generation and discovery progress can move at different speeds. Improving the first does not automatically improve the second.

What needs improvement

Give useful improvements more influence

PPO reached 78.484 by round 12. After 119 rounds, its best score was 78.522, a gain of just 0.038. It kept producing reasonably strong programs but rarely pushed past its early best.

Our reward helps explain why this can happen. Under its exponential transform, a score of 78.48 earns about 0.596 reward; 80.45 earns about 0.626. Avoiding a zero-reward failure offers a much larger gain than finding that better solution. This does not establish the cause of the plateau, but it makes the incentive visible.

Guidance-TTT puts more weight on the strongest outcomes within a parent’s group. I would like to test whether that relative emphasis can improve discovery while retaining PPO’s update constraint. It would change how actor advantages are constructed, so it needs a controlled comparison.

Simply subtracting the parent’s score is less decisive than it sounds. If the critic learns the same shift, reward minus value stays unchanged. The important question is how much influence a useful improvement has on the policy update.

Give the critic a clear job

Our critic predicts the return of the current attempt. It has no training target for what a branch might achieve after several future revisions. A change that opens a promising direction can therefore look unremarkable today.

The first step is to measure whether the baseline reduces gradient variance and assigns sensible advantages to improvements and failures. We also need to compare trained editors on a fixed set of parent programs: in an evolving search, higher scores can come from better starting points as well as better guidance.

A critic that predicts downstream progress is an appealing next step. It would need evidence from longer search trajectories, where we can see which revisions actually enabled later gains.

Make room for successive discoveries

The best Guidance-TTT solution accumulated changes over many rounds:

It remained a greedy packing algorithm, with improvements to ordering, board dimensions, and placement decisions. The gains came from revising an approach repeatedly as new results arrived.

That makes smaller, more frequent batches a useful next experiment. Under the same execution budget, can more feedback rounds help PPO move beyond its early plateau? I want to preserve its ability to produce working changes while giving each new result more chances to shape the next attempt.
entry.summary: Can a model learn to discover better solutions? Recent PPO work and our first experiments with test-time training.
